subject: AI & Agents
title: Expert Systems: Knowledge in a Box
description: A short lesson to help you apply Expert Systems: Knowledge in a Box.

hook.text: By the 1970s, AI researchers tried a new approach: just ask human experts and code their rules.

buildup.text: Expert systems were programs filled with hand-written if-then rules from specialists.

discovery.text: MYCIN diagnosed blood infections better than some doctors using 600 carefully crafted rules.

twist.text: Rules are brittle. One edge case the experts forgot could crash the whole system.

climax.text: Companies spent millions on expert systems that became impossible to maintain.

punchline.text: You can't bottle expertise in if-then statements.

quiz.question: What was a major problem with expert systems?
options: Hand-written rules were brittle and hard to maintain
They were too slow to run

details.summary: Expert systems of the 1970s and 1980s encoded human expert knowledge as if-then rules. Systems like MYCIN diagnosed diseases and XCON configured computers, representing AI's first commercial successes.
details.whyItMatters: Expert systems proved AI could solve real business problems but also revealed the brittleness of hand-coded knowledge. Their limitations motivated the shift toward learning-based approaches.
takeaways: Expert systems encoded human knowledge as if-then rules
They achieved early commercial success in medicine and business
Their brittleness drove the shift toward machine learning

faq.question: What could expert systems actually do?
faq.answer: MYCIN diagnosed bacterial infections with 69% accuracy, matching specialists. XCON configured computer orders at DEC, saving millions annually. They excelled in narrow, well-defined domains with clear rules.

faq.question: Why did expert systems eventually decline?
faq.answer: Maintaining and updating thousands of hand-coded rules proved extremely expensive. They could not handle situations outside their rules and could not learn from new data, limiting their flexibility.
